To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we report three patients with Axenfield–Rieger (A–R) anomaly and various accompanying malformation, and that we suggest that the psychometric retardation is a manifestation of a contiguous gene deletion syndrome.
we report three unrelated Japanese patients who exhibited Axenfeld–Reiger anomalies with various accompanying systemic malformations.

the three Japanese patients with Axr had various systemic anomalies, including cardiac defects, and that the two patients who had deletions of 6p had poor muscle tone and psychomotor delays, suggesting that the psychomotordelay is a clinical manifestation of 6p terminal deletion syndrome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular mechanisms that regulate cell growth and proliferation in the developing retina.
the molecular genetic analysis of Axenfeld‐Rieger syndrome, a rare congenital disorder characterized by anterior segment malformations, dental abnormalities, and systemic malformations.
the development of new methods for the synthesis of biologically active substances, in this case, new compounds of the 2,3-dihydro-4(1H)-quinazolinone series.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Axenfeld–Reiger syndrome (ARS) is caused by mutations in PITX2, FOXC1, and FOXC2.

the 6p deletions in patients with AxR anomalies are associated with the clinical findings of broad forehead, brackyccephaly, hypertolorism, downslanted palpebral fissure, small anteverted nostrils, cardiac defects, autistic features, and developmental retardation.
the clinical phenotype of Axenfeld–Reiger syndrome is highly variable and is dependent on the specific genetic defect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the 6p deletion syndrome, which includes a 6p25 terminal deletion, has a distinct clinical spectrum of extraocular anomalies that is distinct from that of Axenfeld–Reiger syndrome, and that psychomotor retardations are associated with 6p deletions.
the clinical findings in patients with 6p deletions are similar to those of Axenfeld–Reiger syndrome (ARS).
the extraocular findings in our patients are similar to those found with FOXC1 mutation and distinct from those with PITX2 mutation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the 6p deletion syndrome is a clinical entity that is associated with a broad spectrum of clinical findings and that the 6pter–p25 deletion syndrome may be a distinct clinical entity that has psychomotor retardative features.
Axenfeld–Reiger anomalies are associated with a wide range of systemic malformations, which may be caused by a deletion of multiple genes in the 5.0 to 6.6 Mb of the 6p terminal region.
the clinical features of patients with FOXC mutations are distinct from those with PITX2.
